q: What are the three key facts about Canada's system of government?
o: A federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy
A republic, a federal state and a parliamentary democracy
A unitary state, a constitutional monarchy and a direct democracy
A confederation of provinces with an elected head of state
e: Canada is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy.

q: Who is Canada's Head of State?
e: As a constitutional monarchy, Canada's Head of State is a hereditary Sovereign who reigns in accordance with the Constitution. The Prime Minister is the head of government.

q: Who represents the Sovereign in Canada?
e: The Governor General represents the Sovereign in Canada and is appointed on the advice of the Prime Minister, usually for five years.

q: Who represents the Sovereign in each province?
e: In each of the ten provinces the Sovereign is represented by the Lieutenant Governor.

q: In the three territories, who represents the federal government?
e: In the territories, the Commissioner represents the federal government and plays a ceremonial role.

q: What are the three parts of Parliament?
o: The Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the Senate
The Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons
The House of Commons, the courts and the Governor General
The provinces, the territories and the federal government
e: Parliament has three parts: the Sovereign, the Senate and the House of Commons.

q: How are senators chosen?
o: Elected by voters in each province
Appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister
Elected by members of the House of Commons
e: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister and serve until age 75.

q: What must happen before a bill becomes law?
o: It must be approved by a national referendum
It must pass both the House of Commons and the Senate and receive royal assent
It must be signed by every premier
It must be approved by the Supreme Court
e: No bill becomes law until it is passed by both chambers and receives royal assent, granted by the Governor General on behalf of the Sovereign.

q: Which of these is a responsibility of the provinces?
e: Provinces are responsible for education, health, natural resources, property and civil rights, highways and municipal government. Defence, currency and foreign policy are federal.

q: Which two areas do the federal government and the provinces share?
e: The federal government and the provinces share jurisdiction over agriculture and immigration.

q: In what year was the Constitution amended to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms?
e: The Constitution of Canada was amended in 1982 to entrench the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

q: What does habeas corpus mean?
o: The right to vote in secret
The right to challenge unlawful detention by the state
The right to a lawyer paid by the state
The right to live in any province
e: Habeas corpus, the right to challenge unlawful detention by the state, comes from English common law.

q: What do mobility rights mean?
o: Canadians can live and work anywhere they choose in Canada, enter and leave the country freely and apply for a passport
Canadians can drive in any province with one licence
Canadians can move to any country without a visa
Newcomers can choose their province of landing only once
e: Mobility rights let Canadians live and work anywhere in Canada, enter and leave the country freely and apply for a passport.

q: If you are called to serve on a jury, what must you do?
o: You may decline without a reason
You are legally required to serve
You can pay a fee to be excused
e: Serving on a jury is a responsibility of citizenship: when called, you are legally required to serve.

q: Is military service compulsory in Canada?
o: Yes, for all men aged 18 to 25
Yes, for everyone for one year
No, there is no compulsory military service
Only in wartime for new citizens
e: There is no compulsory military service in Canada, although serving in the Canadian Forces is a way to contribute.

q: In what year was Magna Carta signed in England?
e: Canada's tradition of ordered liberty dates back to the signing of Magna Carta in 1215.

q: What is Canada's highest court?
o: The Court of Appeal of Ontario
e: The Supreme Court of Canada is the country's highest court.

q: In which provinces is the RCMP not the provincial police?
e: The RCMP serves as provincial police in all provinces and territories except Ontario and Quebec, which have their own provincial police forces.

q: What does the presumption of innocence mean?
o: Everyone is innocent until proven guilty
Only citizens have a right to a trial
e: Canada's judicial system is founded on the presumption of innocence in criminal matters: everyone is innocent until proven guilty.

q: When was the Dominion of Canada officially born?
e: The Dominion of Canada was officially born on July 1, 1867.

q: Which four provinces formed Canada in 1867?
o: Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick
Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba and British Columbia
Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland
Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and Nova Scotia
e: Ontario and Quebec, together with New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, formed the Dominion of Canada in 1867.

q: Who was Canada's first Prime Minister?
e: In 1867 Sir John Alexander Macdonald, a Father of Confederation, became Canada's first Prime Minister.

q: What happened at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham in 1759?
o: The British defeated the French at Québec City
e: In 1759 the British defeated the French on the Plains of Abraham at Québec City, marking the end of France's empire in America.

q: What was the Underground Railroad?
o: A Christian anti-slavery network that helped slaves escape from the United States to Canada
A secret military supply line in 1812
A tunnel under the Detroit River
e: Thousands of slaves escaped from the United States and settled in Canada via the Underground Railroad, a Christian anti-slavery network.

q: When did Canadian soldiers capture Vimy Ridge?
e: The Canadian Corps captured Vimy Ridge in April 1917.

q: What did the Constitutional Act of 1791 do?
o: It divided the Province of Quebec into Upper Canada and Lower Canada
It made French and English official languages
e: The Constitutional Act of 1791 divided the Province of Quebec into Upper Canada (later Ontario) and Lower Canada (later Quebec).

q: When was the Canadian flag with the maple leaf first raised?
e: A new Canadian flag was raised for the first time in 1965.

q: When was O Canada proclaimed as the national anthem?
e: O Canada was proclaimed as the National Anthem in 1980.

q: What is Canada's national motto, A Mari Usque Ad Mare?
e: After the First World War Canada adopted a coat of arms and the motto A Mari Usque Ad Mare, Latin for "from sea to sea".

q: What is Canada's official summer sport?
e: Lacrosse, an ancient sport first played by Aboriginals, is the official summer sport. Hockey is the national winter sport.

q: What is the highest honour available to Canadians?
e: The Victoria Cross is the highest honour available to Canadians, awarded for the most conspicuous bravery.

q: On what day do Canadians remember the sacrifices of veterans?
e: Each year on November 11, Remembrance Day, Canadians remember the sacrifices of veterans and those who died in war.

q: What are Canada's two official languages?
e: English and French are the two official languages. The Official Languages Act was passed in 1969.

q: What is an electoral district?
o: A province with its own legislature
A geographical area represented by a member of Parliament
e: An electoral district (riding or constituency) is a geographical area represented by a member of Parliament.

q: Who becomes the MP for an electoral district?
o: The candidate chosen by the party leader
The candidate who receives the most votes
The candidate with the most experience
The candidate named by the Governor General
e: The candidate who receives the most votes becomes the MP for that electoral district.

q: What does Canadian law secure for voters?
o: The right to vote by phone
The right to a secret ballot
e: Canadian law secures the right to a secret ballot.

q: Which three oceans line Canada's frontiers?
e: The Pacific Ocean in the west, the Atlantic Ocean in the east and the Arctic Ocean to the north.

q: What is the capital of Canada, and who chose it?
o: Toronto, chosen by Sir John A. Macdonald
Ottawa, chosen by Queen Victoria in 1857
Montréal, chosen by the Fathers of Confederation
e: Ottawa, on the Ottawa River, was chosen as the capital in 1857 by Queen Victoria.

q: Which are the Prairie Provinces?
o: Manitoba, Alberta and the Northwest Territories
e: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are the Prairie Provinces.

q: When was Nunavut established, and what is its capital?
e: Nunavut, meaning "our land" in Inuktitut, was established in 1999. Its capital is Iqaluit.

q: Who is Canada's largest trading partner?
e: Canada and the United States are each other's largest trading partner.

q: Most working Canadians have jobs in which type of industry?
e: More than 75% of working Canadians have jobs in service industries.
